title: The Floor of the Mouth
subtitle: A man in respiratory distress after a toothache, from the emergency department to the ICU
description: Deciding whether a patient in distress can go to CT, choosing how to secure the airway, managing a can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate emergency, reading the CT once it is safe to get one, choosing the definitive airway, and a first-night complication.

steps.title: Step 1/6: The Scanner Is Ready
steps.scenario:
A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a fever and several days of severe pain in a lower molar. He is sitting bolt upright, drooling, with a muffled voice and labored breathing. On room air the saturation is fluctuating between 89 and 92 percent. The floor of his mouth is tense and woody on both sides, and the tongue is pushed up and back.

The emergency physician has booked a contrast CT of the neck and the porter is waiting to take him.
steps.media: Load image: Intraoral photograph of tense, elevated floor of mouth with the tongue displaced upward, consented patient. Caption: 'Floor of mouth.'
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: (A) Send him for the CT; the scan takes five minutes and will show whether there is an abscess to drain
(B) Send him for the CT with a nurse and a pulse oximeter, and intubate afterward if the scan shows airway narrowing
(C) Cancel the scan for now, keep him upright, call anesthesia, and prepare to secure the airway with a surgical airway set open at the bedside
(D) Give intravenous antibiotics and dexamethasone, and reassess in an hour before deciding on imaging

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

He already has the signs of impending obstruction: sitting upright, drooling, muffled voice, labored breathing, and a tongue displaced by bilateral floor-of-mouth swelling. Lying flat in a scanner, away from the people and equipment that can rescue him, is where these patients die. The airway comes first. The CT comes after the tube is in.

Why the others fail:
(A) The scan will not change what happens in the next ten minutes, and it requires him to lie flat with nobody able to intervene.
(B) A nurse and an oximeter cannot secure an airway. A saturation that drops in the scanner is a crisis in the worst possible place.
(D) Antibiotics and steroids are given, but they do not reverse established swelling within an hour, and waiting converts a controlled situation into an emergency one.

Keypoint: a patient with signs of upper airway obstruction does not go to the scanner until the airway is secured.

Reference: Cook TM, Woodall N, Frerk C. Fourth National Audit Project. Br J Anaesth. 2011;106(5):617-631.

steps.title: Step 2/6: Securing the Airway
steps.scenario: He is upright and on high-flow oxygen, but the saturation is still fluctuating between 80 and 89 percent and is not improving. Anesthesia is at the bedside. You are scrubbed with a tracheostomy set open. He is still conscious and can follow instructions.
steps.media: Load image: The double setup as you would stage it: flexible scope and topical anesthesia on one side of the bed, tracheostomy tray open and scalpel-bougie-tube kit laid out on the other. Caption: 'Double setup.'
steps.question: How do you secure the airway?

options.text: (A) Awake flexible fiberoptic nasal intubation with topical anesthesia, with the surgical airway team ready at the neck
(B) Rapid sequence induction with a videolaryngoscope, since he is cooperative and there is no time to topicalize
(C) A nasopharyngeal airway and observation in the resuscitation bay, since he is still moving air
(D) Blind nasal intubation, since the mouth cannot be opened

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

An awake technique keeps him breathing for himself throughout. The scope follows the air passage past the swelling, and if it cannot be done, he is still breathing and the surgical airway can proceed under control. Having the surgeon ready at the neck before starting is the point: the plan for failure is in place before the first attempt.

Why the others fail:
(B) A falling saturation makes this feel urgent, and urgency is the argument for staying awake, not against it. Induction and paralysis remove the muscle tone that is keeping what airway he has open. If the videolaryngoscope cannot pass the swelling, and it often cannot, he is now apneic with an airway you cannot see. Head and neck infection was one of the highest-risk groups for exactly this sequence in the national audit.
(C) A nasopharyngeal airway bypasses the tongue base but not swelling below it, and it can bleed into an already compromised airway. Moving some air at 80 to 89 percent on high-flow oxygen is not a stable airway, and observation is not a plan when the swelling is progressing.
(D) Blind passage through distorted, swollen tissue risks trauma and bleeding and has no way to confirm the route. If the mouth cannot open, that is a reason for a scope, not for going blind.

Keypoint: keep him breathing, look with a scope, and have the neck ready before you start.

Reference: Cook TM, Woodall N, Frerk C. Fourth National Audit Project. Br J Anaesth. 2011;106(5):617-631. Frerk C, Mitchell VS, McNarry AF, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2015 guidelines. Br J Anaesth. 2015;115(6):827-848. doi:10.1093/bja/aev371.

steps.title: Step 3/6: Where Do You Cut
steps.scenario:
The scope reaches the swelling and cannot advance. He becomes agitated, then unresponsive. The saturation reads 60 percent and falling. Bag-valve-mask ventilation does not move the chest. A supraglottic airway does not seat.

You declare a can't-intubate, can't-oxygenate situation.
steps.media: Load image: Your own unlabeled line drawing of the anterior neck: thyroid cartilage, cricoid, thyroid isthmus, tracheal rings. No annotations, no arrows. The same drawing is reused at Step 5. Caption: 'Anterior neck.'
steps.question: Saturation is 60 percent and falling. Where do you cut?

options.text: (A) Through the thyroid cartilage in the midline, the most prominent landmark
(B) Below the cricoid, through the second and third tracheal rings
(C) Needle through the cricothyroid membrane with a large-bore cannula, then jet oxygenation
(D) Through the cricothyroid membrane, between the thyroid cartilage and the cricoid

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The cricothyroid membrane is the most superficial point of the airway. There is no thyroid isthmus over it, it can be felt through the skin even in a swollen neck, and it takes seconds to open. Stabilize the larynx with the non-dominant hand, make a horizontal stab through skin and membrane, rotate the blade, pass a bougie, railroad a 6.0 cuffed tube, inflate the cuff. The Difficult Airway Society names this scalpel technique as the preferred rescue in a can't-intubate, can't-oxygenate emergency.

Why the others fail:
(A) The thyroid cartilage is the landmark you hold, not the one you cut. It is solid cartilage, it does not open into the airway, and cutting it damages the larynx above the folds.
(B) This is the tracheostomy site, and it is right for the definitive airway later. Now it is deeper, under the isthmus, and takes minutes. He has seconds.
(C) About 60 percent of needle attempts failed in the national audit that shaped the 2015 guideline. A cannula gives no cuff, no reliable ventilation, and no protection from aspiration.

Keypoint: the membrane between thyroid cartilage and cricoid is where you cut in an emergency; the tracheal rings are where you cut when there is time.

Reference: Frerk C, Mitchell VS, McNarry AF, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2015 guidelines. Br J Anaesth. 2015;115(6):827-848. doi:10.1093/bja/aev371. Cook TM, Woodall N, Frerk C. Br J Anaesth. 2011;106(5):617-631.

steps.title: Step 4/6: Now the CT
steps.scenario:
The cricothyroidotomy tube is in. Saturation is 99 percent and he is being ventilated. He is now stable enough to lie flat, and the contrast CT of the neck is obtained.

The report reads: swelling of the tongue and tongue base, ill-defined soft tissue density across the floor of the mouth with abscess formation, subcutaneous fat stranding in the submental region consistent with cellulitis, and several inflammatory-appearing nodes in both submandibular regions. No enhancing mass.
steps.media: Load image: Axial and coronal contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, unannotated. Caption: 'Post-contrast.'
steps.question: What does the CT show, and what does it change?

options.text: (A) A peritonsillar abscess; needle aspiration or incision and drainage through the mouth
(B) Bilateral floor-of-mouth infection with abscess formation and surrounding cellulitis; incision and drainage of the floor of the mouth, removal of the source tooth, and intravenous antibiotics
(C) A parapharyngeal abscess; drainage through the neck under general anesthesia
(D) Cellulitis only, with no collection; intravenous antibiotics alone

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The CT confirms the diagnosis and answers the question it was ordered for. Both sides of the floor of the mouth are involved, the tongue base is swollen, which is what was closing the airway, and there is a collection to drain. The plan is incision and drainage of the floor of the mouth, extraction of the source tooth, and intravenous antibiotics covering oral flora. The scan also confirms the infection has not tracked laterally to the parapharyngeal space.

One thing about the report: the findings section describes the collection as ill-defined rather than as a clean rim-enhancing abscess. That is typical of the floor of the mouth, where early pus is loculated and poorly walled off. Read the impression and the clinical picture together, and explore with a low threshold.

Why the others fail:
(A) A peritonsillar abscess sits between the tonsil and the constrictor, on one side, at the level of the oropharynx. This is bilateral and in the floor of the mouth.
(C) A parapharyngeal abscess is lateral to the constrictor near the carotid sheath and would show as an enhancing collection there. The report describes neither.
(D) Antibiotics alone is reasonable for early Ludwig's angina with cellulitis only and no airway compromise. This patient has a collection on the report and has already lost his airway to the infection. Pus is drained.

Keypoint: the CT decides what gets drained; it never decides whether the airway gets secured.

Reference: Vieira F, Allen SM, Stocks RM, Thompson JW. Deep neck infection. Otolaryngol Clin North Am. 2008;41(3):459-483.

steps.title: Step 5/6: The Definitive Airway
steps.scenario: The floor of the mouth is incised and drained and the source tooth is removed. The swelling will take days to settle and he will need the airway for at least a week, so you convert the cricothyroidotomy to a formal tracheostomy in the same sitting.
steps.media: Load image: Your own line drawing of the anterior neck: thyroid cartilage, cricothyroid membrane, cricoid, thyroid isthmus, tracheal rings numbered 1 to 6, innominate artery crossing low. No labels on which level is correct. Caption: 'Anterior neck.'
steps.question: Where do you enter the trachea?

options.text: (A) Through the existing cricothyroidotomy, enlarging the opening
(B) Between the cricoid cartilage and the first tracheal ring
(C) Between the second and third tracheal rings, below the thyroid isthmus
(D) Between the fifth and sixth tracheal rings, as low as possible to keep the tube away from the swelling

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

The tracheostomy goes in below the cricoid, through the second and third rings. The cricoid is the only complete ring in the airway and the narrowest point below the vocal folds. A tube that sits against it, or an opening that damages it, leads to subglottic stenosis that is very hard to treat. The cricothyroidotomy is closed once the tracheostomy is in.

Why the others fail:
(A) This leaves a tube resting on the cricoid for a week or more, which is the stenosis risk the conversion is meant to remove.
(B) Same problem. The cricoid and first ring are protected precisely because injury there produces stenosis at the narrowest part of the airway.
(D) Too low. Below the third or fourth ring the trachea drops behind the sternum, the innominate artery crosses in front of it, and a tube sitting there can erode into the vessel.

Keypoint: below the cricoid, above the innominate, which puts you at rings two and three.

Reference: Mitchell RB, Hussey HM, Setzen G, et al. Clinical consensus statement: tracheostomy care. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2013;148(1):6-20.

steps.title: Step 6/6: The First Night
steps.scenario: He is in the ICU. At 3 a.m. the nurse calls: his neck and upper chest have swollen up over the last hour and crackle on palpation. The ventilator is showing high airway pressures.
steps.media: Load image: Chest radiograph showing subcutaneous air outlining the neck and chest wall muscles, de-identified. Caption: 'Postoperative day 1.'
steps.question: What has most likely happened?

options.text: (A) The skin around the stoma was closed tightly, and air leaking around a partly blocked tube has been forced into the soft tissues
(B) The cuff has been overinflated and is injuring the tracheal wall
(C) The thyroid isthmus was oversewn and is bleeding into the neck
(D) The abscess has re-accumulated and the neck swelling is pus

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

This is subcutaneous emphysema: air in the soft tissues of the neck and chest wall, felt as crepitus under the skin. Air gets there when it cannot get out through the tube, usually because the tube is partly blocked by secretions or malpositioned, and cannot get out around the tube either because the skin is closed tightly around it. The pressure then dissects into the neck and chest and can push the tube out of the trachea. The fix is to check the tube position and patency immediately, and to leave the stoma loosely closed or open in the first place.

Why the others fail:
(B) An overinflated cuff damages the tracheal mucosa over days. It does not put air into the neck in an hour.
(C) Bleeding gives a firm, expanding swelling without crepitus. Air crackles; blood does not.
(D) Re-accumulated pus would be tender, warm and firm, and would not produce crepitus or high ventilator pressures.

Keypoint: subcutaneous emphysema after tracheostomy means air is going the wrong way, and the first check is whether the tube is patent and in the trachea.

Reference: Mitchell RB, Hussey HM, Setzen G, et al. Clinical consensus statement: tracheostomy care. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2013;148(1):6-20.
